title: Conflict resolution
examples: How can I practice active listening in a difficult meeting?
What is the difference between paraphrasing and reframing?
Can you give me a scenario where reframing is very helpful?

explain.say: Today we are learning two key skills for tough conversations. These skills are active listening and reframing. They help us understand better and communicate clearer.
Active listening means fully concentrating on what the other person is saying. It is more than just waiting for your turn to speak. You show you are paying attention with your body and words.
A good way to show you listened is to paraphrase what you heard. You can say something like, so I hear you saying that you feel overwhelmed.

items: I hear you saying | You feel overwhelmed

explain.say: Reframing is taking a negative statement and changing its focus. You shift the conversation to a more constructive or positive angle. It changes the meaning without changing the facts.

draw.text: Change the focus, keep the facts.

explain.say: Imagine a colleague says, you never help with the reports. You can reframe that to focus on teamwork needs. You could say, perhaps we could divide the report sections differently.
In a real work meeting, if someone says, this project will fail because of the budget. You can reframe it by asking, what specific budget constraints are causing the most concern?

faq.q: What is the difference between paraphrasing and reframing?
faq.a: Paraphrasing repeats the core message using your own words to confirm understanding. Reframing changes the perspective or focus of the message to make it more productive.
asks: How do I show I understood correctly?
Is repeating what they say the same as changing the topic?

faq.q: When should I use active listening in a disagreement?
faq.a: You should use it at the very beginning of the disagreement. It helps both people feel heard before any solutions are discussed.
asks: Do I need to agree with them to listen well?
Is it better to listen first or suggest a solution first?

faq.q: Can I reframe something that is factually untrue?
faq.a: Reframing should always be based on facts you have heard. You are changing the interpretation of the facts, not changing the facts themselves.
asks: Can I change what they said?

faq.q: What if the other person keeps interrupting me?
faq.a: You can use a calm, active listening technique by saying, please let me finish my point first. You can also ask them to write down their thoughts.
asks: How do I get them to stop talking over me?
What is a polite way to take control of the conversation?

faq.q: Are these skills only for personal relationships?
faq.a: No, these are essential professional skills. They improve how you manage team conflicts and client expectations in any job setting.
asks: Do I use this at work?

facts: Active listening requires non-verbal cues like eye contact.
Reframing shifts focus from blame to action.
A goal of conflict resolution is mutual understanding.

quiz.say: A colleague says, 'Your report was messy and hard to read.' Which response best uses reframing?
quiz.show: A. You are right, I will fix it.

options.show: B. What structural changes can we make to improve clarity?
options.say: B. What structural changes can we make to improve clarity?

options.show: A. You are right, I will fix it.
options.say: A. You are right, I will fix it.

options.show: C. It was fine when I gave it to you.
options.say: C. It was fine when I gave it to you.

options.show: D. You should read the instructions better.
options.say: D. You should read the instructions better.

quiz.why: This shifts the focus from personal failure to a solvable process issue.

wrong.1: This accepts blame immediately, which doesn't solve the underlying process problem.
wrong.2: This becomes defensive and shuts down further constructive conversation.
wrong.3: This is accusatory and violates the goal of mutual understanding.

quiz.say: When someone speaks quickly and emotionally, what is the best initial active listening technique?

options.show: D. Interrupt with a related point.
options.say: D. Interrupt with a related point.

options.show: B. Let me summarize what I hear you saying.
options.say: B. Let me summarize what I hear you saying.

options.show: A. Tell them to slow down.
options.say: A. Tell them to slow down.

quiz.why: Summarizing shows deep attention and gives you time to process the emotion.

wrong.0: Nodding alone does not confirm that you have actually processed the content.
wrong.1: This breaks the flow and makes the speaker feel unheard.
wrong.3: This is directive and can sound dismissive of their feelings.

quiz.say: A team member says, 'This whole project is impossible because of the timeline.' What is the most effective reframed question?

options.show: B. We just need more time to finish it.
options.say: B. We just need more time to finish it.

options.show: D. Maybe we should rethink the scope entirely.
options.say: D. Maybe we should rethink the scope entirely.

options.show: C. What specific milestones are currently blocking progress?
options.say: C. What specific milestones are currently blocking progress?

options.show: A. Why do you think it is impossible?
options.say: A. Why do you think it is impossible?

quiz.why: This moves the discussion from a general feeling of impossibility to concrete, actionable steps.

wrong.0: This is a suggestion, not a question, and avoids analyzing the root cause.
wrong.1: This is too drastic and jumps to a conclusion without gathering facts first.
wrong.3: This forces them into a defensive explanation rather than a solution.
